CONTEXT / HARNESS NOTE for all evidence below. Every `input` field is the exact string passed to markdown.markdown() (it is "## Section 1
" + args.a, and args.a always began with "

" so the list is an isolated document). Every `output` field is the exact, complete return value of markdown.markdown() for that input — no trailing newline. Interior newlines are shown as

BLOCK SPLITTING AND DISPATCH. The document text is split into blocks on the literal separator "

" (`text.split('

')`), producing a mutable FIFO list. The parser repeatedly takes blocks[0], walks the processor registry in this fixed priority order — empty(100), listindent(90), code(80), hashheader(70), setextheader(60), hr(50), olist(40), ulist(30), blockquote(20), reference(15), paragraph(10) — and runs the first whose test() returns true; run() pops blocks[0] and may push new blocks at index 0. Because olist has higher priority than ulist, an `ol` marker on the first line wins. Because hr(50) and setextheader(60) outrank both list processors, a block whose first line is a list item but which also looks like a setext header or contains an HR line is NOT a list.

OL BLOCK TEST. A block is an ordered list iff `/^ {0,3}\d+\.[ ]+(.*)/` matches the block (regex is NOT multiline and IS anchored, so this tests only the first line). `\d` is Python's Unicode-aware digit class: it matches any Unicode decimal-digit (category Nd), not just ASCII 0-9. At least one SPACE must follow the dot. Leading indent must be 0-3 spaces (4+ goes to listindent/code). Container tag is `<ol>`.

UL BLOCK TEST. A block is an unordered list iff `/^ {0,3}[*+-][ ]+(.*)/` matches the block (anchored, first line only). `*`, `+`, `-` are all equivalent markers. At least one SPACE must follow the marker; 0-3 leading spaces allowed. Container tag is `<ul>`. A marker with no following space is not a marker.

NO `start` ATTRIBUTE, EVER. The ol start value is parsed internally but `LAZY_OL` is True, so `<ol>` is emitted with no attributes regardless of the first number. Numbering of subsequent items is likewise ignored; the item order in the source is the item order in the output.

ITEM SPLITTING (get_items). Once a block is claimed by the ol or ul processor, the block is split into item strings by scanning its lines in order with these three regexes (identical for ol and ul):
  CHILD  = /^ {0,3}((\d+\.)|[*+-])[ ]+(.*)/
  INDENT = /^ {4,7}((\d+\.)|[*+-])[ ]+.*/
Algorithm: items = []; for each line of block.split('\n'):
  1. if CHILD matches -> items.push(CHILD group 3)  [i.e. leading indent AND marker AND all following spaces are dropped]
  2. else if INDENT matches -> if items[last] starts with 4 spaces, items[last] += '\n' + line (RAW line, indentation kept); else items.push(line) (RAW line).
  3. else -> items[last] += '\n' + line (RAW line, indentation kept).
Note consequences: (a) the marker CHARACTER is irrelevant after the first line — `*`, `-`, `+` and `N.` all start a new item in the same container, so a container never switches from ul to ol or vice versa mid-block; (b) a marker line indented 8+ spaces does NOT match INDENT (`[ ]{4,7}` cannot reach it) and falls to rule 3, becoming a literal continuation line; (c) all spaces between the marker and the text are consumed, so `*     a` yields item text `a`.

LAZY / INDENTED CONTINUATION LINES (no blank line). Any line inside the block that is neither a CHILD nor an INDENT match is appended verbatim (including its own leading spaces) to the current item with a '\n' separator. Because the item is then re-parsed as a single block in 'list' state, the result is that the raw text — original interior indentation and all — becomes the `<li>` text. 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4+ spaces of continuation indent all behave identically (the spaces are preserved in the output, not stripped).

CONTAINER PLACEMENT (list processor run(), case A — fresh list). If the last child of the current parent element is NOT an `ol`/`ul`, and the parent itself is not an `ol`/`ul`, a new container (`<ol>` or `<ol>`/`<ul>` per the first-line marker) is appended to the parent. Then for each item string: if the item starts with exactly 4 spaces, it is parsed with the container's LAST `<li>` as parent (nesting); otherwise a new `<li>` is appended and the item is parsed into it. Throughout this loop the parser state is 'list'.

A LIST DIRECTLY AFTER A PARAGRAPH LINE WITH NO BLANK LINE IS NOT A LIST. Since blocks are split only on "

", `para
* a
* b` is a single block whose first line is not a marker, so the paragraph processor swallows the whole thing verbatim. Contrast: after a hash header in the same block, the header processor pushes the remainder back as a new block, so the list IS recognised.

TIGHT ITEMS (parser state 'list'). While a list item block is being parsed, the paragraph processor does NOT create a `

  • `. If sibling exists, the block is appended to sibling.tail (' '+block, or sibling.tail+' '+block if the tail is already set). If there is no child, the block is appended to li.text (li.text = block.lstrip() if li.text was empty, else li.text + ' ' + block). This is why tight items render as `
  • text
    • ` with no `

    `, and why a header followed by a lazy line renders as `

  • H

    text
    • `.

LOOSE LISTS (case B — sibling merge). If the last child of the parent IS an `ol` or `ul` (either tag; the sibling set is ['ol','ul'] for both processors), the new block's items are merged into THAT existing container rather than creating a new one. Three things happen, in order: (1) If the container's last `
  • ` has non-empty .text, that text is moved into a NEW `

    ` inserted as child index 0 of that `

  • ` and li.text is set to '' — this retroactively makes the PREVIOUS item loose. (2) Let lch = last child of that `
  • `. If lch exists and lch.tail is non-empty, a `

    ` is appended to the `

  • ` with text = lch.tail.lstrip() and lch.tail is cleared. (3) A new `
  • ` is appended and ONLY THE FIRST item of the new block is parsed into it with state 'looselist' (so the paragraph processor DOES create a `

    `). The state is then reset and the REMAINING items of the block are parsed in normal 'list' (tight) state. Consequences: with `* a * b` both items become loose; with `* a * b * c` only b and c become loose while a stays tight; with `* a * b * c` only a and b become loose while c stays tight. Because the sibling set spans both tags, a blank line between a `ul` block and an `ol` block merges them into the FIRST container's tag. Two or more consecutive blank lines behave the same as one (the intervening empty block is consumed by the empty-block processor without changing the last child).

MULTI-PARAGRAPH ITEMS REQUIRE 4-SPACE INDENT AFTER THE BLANK LINE. A block after a blank line only rejoins the list if it starts with at least 4 spaces (see the listindent rule). With 0-3 spaces of indent it becomes an ordinary sibling block at the parent level and does NOT continue the item; the list is closed, and a following `* c` then starts a brand-new `
    ` (its last-child sibling is now a `

LISTINDENT PROCESSOR — TEST. Priority 90 (runs before code(80)). It claims blocks[0] iff ALL of: (a) the block starts with 4 spaces; (b) the parser is not currently in the 'detabbed' state; (c) either the current parent's tag is 'li', OR the parent has at least one child and its LAST child's tag is 'ul' or 'ol'. Condition (c) is what makes a 4-space-indented block after a list rejoin the list while the same block after a paragraph becomes a code block.

LISTINDENT PROCESSOR — get_level / looseDetab. Let `INDENT_RE = /^(( {4})+)/`; indent_level = (length of match group 1)/4 if it matches else 0 (note: only whole groups of 4 count, so 5,6,7 spaces all give 1 and 8..11 give 2). level = 1 if the current state is 'list' else 0. Then: while indent_level > level: child = last child of parent; if child exists and child.tag is one of ul/ol/li: { if child.tag is ul or ol then level += 1; parent = child } else break. Returns (level, parent). The block is then de-indented by `looseDetab(block, level)`: for each line INDEPENDENTLY, if the line starts with exactly `4*level` spaces those spaces are removed, otherwise the line is left completely unchanged.

LISTINDENT PROCESSOR — RUN dispatch. After computing (level, sibling) and de-indenting, the state 'detabbed' is pushed (which blocks re-entry of this processor for nested parses) and exactly one branch fires: 1. if the ORIGINAL parent.tag == 'li': if that li has children and its last child is ul/ol -> parse the block into that nested list; else parse the block into the li itself. 2. elif sibling.tag == 'li' -> parse the block into that li. NOTE: no `

  • b
    …` with `b` NOT wrapped in `
    `.
  3. elif sibling has children and its last child is 'li' -> FIRST, if that li has non-empty .text, move the text into a new `

Inside a single list block, exactly 4,5,6 or 7 leading spaces before a marker create one nesting level (the whole 4-space prefix is stripped by looseDetab, so 5/6/7 spaces leave 1/2/3 residual spaces which the child's own `[ ]{0,3}` allows).
